input: Research sleep study clinics for chronic insomnia

keyUnknowns.whyItMatters: Knowing whether this is for the user themselves or someone else (e.g. a child, partner, elderly parent) changes which clinics are relevant, as some specialize by age group or patient type.
Location determines which clinics are geographically accessible — results for in-person visits are entirely location-dependent.
Insurance coverage or budget limits which clinics are financially viable, since sleep studies can be expensive and not all clinics accept all plans.
Knowing whether the goal is just a diagnostic sleep study (polysomnography) or also ongoing treatment (e.g. CBT-I, medication management) defines how broadly to research.
Whether the user needs an in-person overnight study or is open to a home sleep test or telehealth consultation affects which clinic types to prioritize.
Understanding what a 'good' clinic looks like to the user — accreditation, wait times, specialist credentials, patient reviews — focuses the research on the right quality signals.
Some users prefer a specific treatment philosophy (e.g. non-medication approaches like CBT-I vs. pharmacological) which would steer them toward different types of practitioners or clinics.

gold.taskTitle: Research sleep study clinics for chronic insomnia
gold.taskDescription: Find and evaluate sleep study clinics that can assess and treat chronic insomnia.

questions.title: Who is the sleep study being researched for?
questions.description: Identify whether this is for the user themselves or another person (e.g. a child, partner, or elderly parent), as clinic specializations vary by patient demographic.

questions.title: What city or region should the clinics be located in?
questions.description: Determine the geographic area so that only accessible, local clinics are included in the research.

questions.title: Is there a specific insurance plan or budget to work within?
questions.description: Establish financial constraints so that only covered or affordable clinics are shortlisted, since sleep studies can be costly.

questions.title: Is the goal diagnosis only, or also ongoing insomnia treatment?
questions.description: Clarify the scope — whether to find clinics for a one-time diagnostic study or clinics that also offer treatment programs like CBT-I or medication management.

questions.title: Is an in-person overnight study required, or is remote an option?
questions.description: Determine whether the user needs a lab-based polysomnography, is open to a home sleep test, or would consider a telehealth consultation, as this changes which clinic formats to research.

questions.title: What makes a clinic count as a strong candidate to you?
questions.description: Identify the user's key quality signals — such as AASM accreditation, short wait times, specialist credentials, or patient reviews — to focus research on what matters most.

questions.title: Do you prefer non-medication approaches over pharmacological ones?
questions.description: Understand the user's treatment philosophy preference, such as favoring CBT-I or sleep hygiene programs versus clinics that lean toward medication, to steer research accordingly.
